en: The Mahātejas-dhāraṇī Sūtra, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of North India during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavat was staying in the great city of Śrāvastī at the Jetavana Grove.
At the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery,
together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus,
there were also immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
Surrounded on all sides by the fourfold assembly,
the World-Honored One then addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying: "Ānanda!"
There is a dharani-dharma-sūtra which the Buddhas of the past have already revealed,
providing both concise and extensive explanations for the sake of their attendants and all sentient beings so that they may attain peace and happiness.
Out of compassion for the world’s devas and humans and for the sake of their extensive benefit,
I now likewise wish to proclaim this dhāraṇī,
so that all sentient beings may experience peace and happiness.
Out of compassion for the world’s devas and humans, and for the sake of their extensive benefit,
Ānanda, since you have been my personal attendant, serving me intimately—
I shall now explain this fundamental teaching for you.
Listen attentively, receive it with care, and reflect upon it well;
I will speak for you.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One;
I wish and desire to hear [it]."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"First is supernormal power;
second is the fundamental."
Furthermore, first is the perfection of aspiration;
second is the perfection of vision;
yet they do not enter nirvana.
These are the view of annihilationism and the view of eternalism.
Furthermore, there are two views that do not lead to nirvana:
namely, the view of a self and the view of attachment to afflictions.
From the perspective of one who possesses wisdom,
it is called "non-wisdom. Furthermore,
it should be understood that this refers to worldly affairs as well as attachment to conventional expressions.
One should know what is a thing and what is not a thing;
one should know conditioned things and unconditioned things;
one should know arising and one should know cessation.
Then one should know the points of entry,
one should know the non-points of entry,
and one should know the points of departure.
One should know the place of departure;
one should know the location;
one should know craving.
One should know the causal condition of craving;
one should know the path of the objective sphere;
one should know the destination where [craving] arises and departs.
One should know the bases of entry;
one should know the excellence of the destination and the departure;
and one should know separation.
One should know the dwelling of separation;
one should know the gathering of non-activities;
one should know speech that is not meaningful.
One should know the collection of phenomena;
one should know conditions;
and one should know the locus of conditions.
One should know the harmony of conditions;
one should know the locus of the arising of conditions;
one should know the arising from conditions.
One should know the phenomena produced by conditions;
one should know conduct;
and one should know superior conduct.
One should know the roots of goodness that abide in the realm;
one should know the accomplishment of gathering leisure;
and one should know the attainment of the factors conducive to leisure.
One should know that the roots of goodness for the appearance of a Buddha in the world have been attained;
one should know how to perform acts of protection;
and one should know that faith and aspiration are diminishing.
One should know the secluded place;
one should know the two kinds of solitary mastery:
that which arises from individual discernment and that which arises from others.
One should know that there are three kinds of causes and conditions for attainment,
which correspond to the practice of the three trainings,
and two kinds of pure ethical discipline.
There are three kinds of sacred teachings:
first, those characterized by attachment and aversion;
second, those that are true, namely the teaching of the Tathāgata.
A single friend is not to be broken;
a single companion may enter a place of fear together with you.
All sentient beings are independent; they are not true spiritual friends.
All sentient beings possess the difficulty of being unresponsive to the practice of faith;
all sentient beings have a nature that is subject to destruction;
all sentient beings share a single common course of action.
Because all sentient beings cannot attain love, they become slaves to craving.
Because all sentient beings do not see their own transgressions, they do not enter nirvana.
Because all sentient beings mutually obstruct one another, they do not attain liberation.
Because a single root of goodness cannot sever [the continuity], one enters parinirvāṇa;
yet, having performed various karmas, they are not lost or destroyed.
Because one enters into a single desire, one enters an evil destination.
Because of entering into the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth desires, one enters into hell.
There is one kind of non-desire;
there is one kind of seal.
There are two kinds of observation:
one is courageous vigor,
and the other is the path of the seven stations.
The five factors that destroy the five powers;
the five bases of verbal expression;
and the five worldly dharmas.
The five destinies of rebirth,
the five aggregates,
and the five ailments.
The five states of health,
the five faculties,
and the five times.
The five samaya portions,
the five mahotsavas,
and the five final moments of mind are brought forth from their place of origin.
The five dharmas of non-victory,
the five types of the weak and timid,
and the five kinds of upāsakas.
The five types of those with excessive greed,
the five types of officials,
and the five immeasurables.
The five superior activities,
the five discursive proliferations,
and the five terrors.
Five types of enemies,
five things not shared with the mind,
and five things that are not respected.
The five things to be honored,
the five things to be respected,
and the five things to be borne.
The five fears,
the five harmonies of the officials,
and the five kinds of cessation based on the body.
Five kinds of cessation depend on speech;
five kinds of cessation depend on the mind;
and there are five kinds of causal conditions for perception.
The five feelings,
the severance of the five feelings,
and the five darknesses.
The five blind ones of darkness;
the five cataracts that obscure the eyes;
the five rākṣasas.
Five abysses,
five whirlpools,
and five caves.
The five interruptions;
the first dhyāna of the fivefold division;
the five kinds of sounds.
The five kinds of worldly dharmas;
the five kinds of common dharmas for raising charges;
and the five instructions.
The five teachings of the spiritual friends;
the five kinds of sources from which the sounds of the Dharma discourse arise;
and the five kinds of methods of debate.
The five faculties of joy,
the five bases for the arising of joy,
and the five factors that give rise to sorrow.
The five types of timidity and fear should be explained;
the five kinds of functional capacities should be explained;
and the five kinds of worldly meritorious conduct should be explained.
The five kinds of outflowing phenomena (āsrava-dharma) come together;
the five kinds of superior worldly conduct;
and the five kinds of contact-born [phenomena].
The five kinds of evil destinies,
the five kinds of evil eyes,
and the five kinds of evil ears.
Five kinds of evil noses,
five kinds of evil tongues,
and five kinds of evil bodies.
The five kinds of malicious intent,
the five dharmas devoid of merit,
and the five causes and conditions for solitary dwelling.
The five ways of departing from a teacher and following conditions;
the five dharmas that should accord with the assembly;
and the causal conditions for the five types of sensation.
The five feelings are not severed or extinguished;
these five factors should be regarded as sorrow.
Because one is attached to the five types of pain and does not fully comprehend them, one experiences suffering and anguish.
The five kinds of hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are not to be grasped;
the five kinds of obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are to be analyzed.
First, the practice of one-sided dharmas should not be grasped.
Five kinds of things should be abandoned;
five characteristics are not subject to cessation;
five dry things arise without cause.
The five places where evil is committed;
the five kinds of smoke;
and the five types of deceitful and fraudulent speech.
There are five kinds of thieves difficult to strike down even with long life;
there are five things practiced at the time of action;
and there are five kinds of sentient beings who are equal in the cemetery.
There are five conditions for dwelling in empty places;
five reasons for not being afraid while in caves;
and five reasons for being resolute and not committing evil.
The five skillful practices constitute the sphere of activity;
the five are without interval;
and the five dharmas do not create differentiation.
The five abodes; the five evil abodes;

the five kinds of obtaining money and goods, obtaining the recollection of past lives, obtaining mindfulness and wisdom, realizing through direct vision, and skillfully turning in accordance with causes and conditions.
The five non-poisons,
the five moist purifications (ārdra-paryāya),
and the five roots of goodness that follow along with their great fruition.
The five qualities of relinquishment,
the five matters of indolence,
and the five fulfillments of faith.
When the five dharmas are fully perfected, one shall enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The five faculties first receive their karmic retribution;
the fivefold accumulation of wisdom then proceeds toward fulfillment.
The roots of goodness from giving at these five times mature and increase;
through these five kinds of giving, one shall diminish all states of existence;
and through these five kinds of precepts, one transcends them.
The five paths are fulfilled.
The five precepts are all well-guarded and fulfilled.
These five kinds of precepts are for turning the wheel of Dharma.
Having fully observed the five precepts,
one attains forty kinds of joyful dharmas;
having received all five precepts.
Those who are weak and inferior, whose precepts are incomplete, deficient,
or violated— namely, upāsakas and upāsikās—
encounter these five kinds of thorns and afflictions at the time of death.
One should fully perfect the five kinds of skillful liberation;
the five kinds of middle and extreme [practices];
and the five kinds of weakness in the precepts.
The inverted practice of the five precepts is no different [from their correct practice].
For those whose five precepts are weak, one should preach [the Dharma] for them.
Those who possess the five precepts together should turn the wheel of the twelve aspects.
There are five kinds of time, which are one: the time of the Dharma.
There are five kinds of speech, which are one: the speech of the Dharma.
There are five kinds of assemblies, which are one: the assembly of the congregation.
Of the five kinds of paths, one is wholesome and sublime;
of the five modes of death, one is cessation;
of the five types of knowledge, one is supreme.
I praise the oneness of the five objects;
the five paths have no distinct characteristics;
and among the five liberations, there is not even one that transcends.
The five realities are one true reality;
the five kinds of cessation are one true cessation;
the five kinds of evil are beyond purification.
The five kinds of exultation,
the five kinds of self-indulgence,
and the five kinds of disciplinary punishment.
The dwelling of Āraṇya possesses five praises.
One who sits at the head [of the assembly] obtains the five praises;
one who constantly practices alms-gathering while walking at the head [of the procession] obtains the five praises.
The five ways of entering a village should be taught;
the five merits of sewing robes;
and the five merits of one who is learned and delights in the Dharma.
There are five merits;
five kinds of evil Māras, Pāpīyas, create obstacles;
and five kinds of afflictive hindrances that obstruct the teaching of the Dharma, the speaking of the Dharma, and the completion of its practice.
The five matters of liberation from evil,
the five obstacles to attainment,
and the five destructions.
The five worldly thieves,
the five types of acquisitive speech,
and the five matters of false speech.
The five [grounds of] non-cohabitation,
the five [grounds of] relinquishing knowledge,
and the five evils of breaking the precepts.
There are five bases for the breaking of the precepts;
five ways of understanding the distinctions regarding the breaking of the precepts;
and five matters for upholding the Vinaya.
One should know that there are five types of conceptualizers who do not uphold the Vinaya;
one should know that there are five types of bhikṣus who do not understand proper decorum and do not uphold the Vinaya,
yet on account of their speech, they claim for themselves to be widely learned.
In such and such a way,
that practitioner of the holy life does not inquire about the five dharmas while upholding the Vinaya.
One who is fiercely prone to anger will head toward the evil destinies.
Among the five types of those who uphold the Vinaya,
there is one who possesses afflictions yet feels no shame or remorse.
One may obtain five kinds of dry [semen] while practicing intentional emission of impurity and yet claim it to be pure.
When practicing the observance of the Vinaya, one incurs five kinds of offenses and five kinds of untimely speech.
There are five kinds of faults in seeking a reward for the gift of the Dharma,
and five kinds of roots of contention that cause fear among bhikṣus.
The five foul and impure dharmas are not the speech of those in training.
Because they are oppressed by the five kinds of teachers, they revile the Buddha.
There are five ways of reviling the Dharma.
There are five ways of disparaging the Saṃgha.
The Dharma Master has five kinds of impurity.
A bhikṣu should know whether these are distinct from one another or not.
There are five kinds of factors that lead to frivolous conduct.
One who does not maintain the precepts, whose body is characterized by breaking the precepts, becomes a speaker of falsehood;
furthermore, there are others who speak falsely.
Precepts are like excrement and filth.
A bhikṣu who is fully endowed with five qualities has a mind as turbulent as the wind.
A bhikṣu who is fully endowed with five qualities speaks the words of non-Buddhists.
If a bhikṣu is endowed with five qualities, he will not be skillful in knowing the sūtras.
If a bhikṣu is endowed with five qualities, he will abandon the Buddha’s bodhi.
If a bhikṣu is endowed with five qualities, he will be able to give rise to anger.
Once anger has arisen, one abandons the Buddha’s words.
A layperson may be fully endowed with five qualities that accord with the Dharma for a renunciant teacher.

[There are also] the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), the five upper fetters (*pañca ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), the five corruptions (*pañca āghātāḥ*), and the five evils (*pañca pāpakāni*).
The five bodily fetters, the five afflictive dharmas,
the five causes and five conditions,
the five summits and falls, and the five modes of non-sovereignty.
5. The signs of imminent fall for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
4. The assembly rites of the Cāturmahārājika gods;
5. The acceptance [of offerings] by the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
1. The gods of the Thirty-three do not accept [gifts].
2. For the gods of the Thirty-three, the maturation of their karma is superior to wine.
3. The goddesses of the Five Excellent Dharmas abandon their own *devaputra* and turn toward another god.
Five thousand three hundred devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, including Śakradevendra and Nirmāṇarati, accompanied by twelve thousand celestial maidens, departed from the Sudharma Hall.
These five thousand three hundred devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven assembled, desiring to defeat the asuras.
The five [classes of] Trāyastriṃśa gods arrive at the grove with signs of conflict.
One should know that the five [classes of] Trāyastriṃśa gods initiate the battle;
the five [classes of] Trāyastriṃśa gods, being endowed with the Dharma, defeat the asuras.
The gods of the Thirty-three Heavens possess the dharma of vigor;
as soon as they are born, they immediately conceive this thought and attain the knowledge of their own karma.
The great assemblies of the devas who practice the five kinds of sensual desires;
the five kinds of devas in the Yāma heaven who, through faith and skillful means, are born to behold the Buddhas;
and the Yāma devas who possess five kinds of past roots of goodness.
They sport without becoming deluded.
The gods of the Yāma heaven, who possess five kinds of roots of merit from the past,
are each free from arrogance and free from envy.
The gods of the Yāma heaven, having transcended all idleness, are endowed with five qualities.
They are fully possessed of these five dharmas.
The devaputras of Tuṣita shall attain ninety-nine kinds of dharmas of joy;
five kinds of devaputras of Tuṣita, through their former vows, shall not lose right mindfulness.
The five classes of devaputras of Tuṣita do not become deluded regarding the dharmas of their former vows,
because they have fulfilled the precepts of their fivefold former superior vows.
The devaputras of Tuṣita have accomplished supernormal powers because their vows are fulfilled.
Through discernment,
the fivefold dharma is fully accomplished.
The devaputras of Tuṣita encounter the Buddha’s birth.
Because they do not abandon what has already been attained and are fully endowed with faith,
they leave the household life to go forth and draw near to the Tathāgata.
Having gone forth, they attain the wisdom of liberation.
Endowed with these five qualities,
the devaputras of Tuṣita abide in the dharma of the signs of imminent death;
though they are born, they do not fear death.
After death, without needing to apply deliberate thought, one knows the place of rebirth;
one is able to give rise to weary detachment and does not become negligent,
being fully endowed with seventy-five kinds of marks.
The Tushita devaputras excel in the practice of desire;
they are endowed with fifteen kinds of marks.
When the various devaputras of Tushita encounter the birth of a Buddha, [they rejoice].
They will draw near [to the Buddha] without ever departing and will never give rise to regret.
If they do not encounter a Buddha at the end of their lives, when they are subsequently reborn among humans, they shall attain renunciation and realize the path of a pratyekabuddha.
The wise should know that those with the marks of the five sense-faculties who have passed away from the Tuṣita devas are reborn among humans;
likewise, those with the marks of the five sense-faculties who have passed away from the Yāma devas [are reborn among humans].
The appearance of five faculties indicates the end of life for those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
the appearance of five faculties indicates the end of life for those among the gods of the Four Great Kings;
the appearance of three faculties indicates the end of life for the various gods dwelling on earth.
One who dies among humans with eight types of faculties will be reborn among humans;
the wise should know that there are six types of faculties.
Having been gathered in the Great Universal Hell,
one dies and is reborn among humans;
the wise should recognize and grasp this sign.
Those with nine root-signs die in the Great Hell of Mutual Life;
those with seven root-signs die in the Great Hell of Black Rope;
those with thirteen root-signs undergo rapid transformation, rapid extinction, and rapid rebirth.
Those with the four root-signs die in the cold hells and are reborn among humans;
those with the four root-signs die among animals;
those with the four root-signs die among monkeys and are reborn among humans.
The mark of the six sense organs is death among jackals and rebirth among humans;
the mark of the sixteen sense organs is death among true lions and rebirth among humans.
These four types of marks of the sense organs occur during the first part of the day.
The four types of signs of the faculties during the middle part of the day;
the four types of signs of the faculties during the latter part of the day;
and the four types of signs of the faculty of hatred.
Ānanda, I have spoken briefly for now.
If you wish to clarify this meaning in detail, [you should listen].
There are twelve koṭis of hundreds of thousands of such superior faculties.
That Buddha-Tathāgata knows the specific number of faculties for each and every sentient being, Ānanda.
There may be someone who, at the first part of the day, should have attained the exhaustion of outflows,
but because they were not instructed and thus failed to relinquish [their attachments],
they commit an act of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma) and bring it to full completion during the middle part of the day.
For this reason, Ānanda,
they turn their backs on the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and fall into the great hells.
There are some people who, at the first part of the day, receive instruction in the Buddha-dharma.
Because they are endowed with desire,
once that person has sat down in that place, they attain such a state of mind through right mindfulness.
Just as those who slander the Buddhas or disparage bodhi fall into the midst of the heterodox,
Ānanda, there are sentient beings who desire to take up robes.
"Ānanda, when one who is free from desire puts on his robes,
there are beings who, while still possessed of desire, lift up their feet."
Setting down his feet free from desire,
Ānanda, there are sentient beings who, while thinking of sensual desires, fall asleep.
Once he had sat upon the couch, he immediately attained the destruction of the outflows.
Ānanda, there are sentient beings who, when overcome by desire, go to lie down.
Before his head has even reached the pillow,
he attains freedom from desire in the interval;
such is the case for sentient beings who have not yet gone forth into homelessness.
Within the Buddha's teaching, one ought to be reborn in the heavens;
yet, having gone forth [into homelessness], one falls into the great hells and reaches the Place of No Joy.
This is because there are sentient beings who do not go forth.
One should fall into the great hells and reach the place of no joy;
however, one who has gone forth and attained the supreme knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows should recognize such signs as these.
Ānanda, if the householder Sudatta had not gone forth after seven days had passed,
[he would have become a wheel-turning monarch].
They should fall into the Great Hell of Unrelenting Torment (Avīci), a place of great displeasure. Ānanda,
the Tathāgata possesses such wisdom that knows the various faculties (indriya) of beings, each being distinct.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is able to know the places from which sentient beings come and the places to which they go;
he also skillfully knows the distinct states of their faculties. Ānanda!
Observe that women possess the quality of joy;
one knows whether they are subject to lust or free from lust by observing their facial expressions through the predominance of their faculties.
How much less could the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—
who has realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—
not know such superior characteristics of the faculties of sentient beings?
The Tathāgata possesses such great power and such great wisdom, Ānanda.
There are sentient beings for whom the Tathāgata,
having entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms during the first part of the day, arrives at the second set of four continents by that time,
remaining in those intermediate regions.
At the first division of the day, for the sake of skillfully converting a single sentient being by means of forty kinds of signs,
he was still in the great city of Śrāvastī, begging for alms in sequence.
In the great city of Śrāvastī, there were sixty sentient beings whose faculties were impaired and who had committed the acts of immediate retribution;
they had committed unrighteous deeds with the intent to kill their mothers.
"If those beings were to go forth from the household life,
they would immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
Having spoken these words, [he remained silent].
Then the Elder Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
for what cause and condition [do you say this]?"
The Tathāgata, for the sake of a single sentient being,
employs forty kinds of skillful means to teach and transform them in that place;
yet he is likewise able to do so in the great city of Śrāvastī.
"Does he cause all sentient beings to act without obstruction within the noble Dharma?
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"That one sentient being is in a world-system of four great continents in the second set of four continents."
Regarding the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One,
who teaches and transforms beings through forty kinds of skillful means:
is it only the Buddha who can deliver them, and not the śrāvakas?
If, during the first part of that day,
the Tathāgata does not convert even a single sentient being,
he would be as one who has committed all five deeds of immediate retribution.
They shall fall into the Avīci Great Hell;
having fallen into hell, they will undergo great suffering for nine hundred and ninety *koṭis* of hundreds of thousands of years.
Those sentient beings can only be converted by a Buddha.
Not by any other vehicle, Ānanda;
that single sentient being is the very last to be delivered.
"Only the Buddha can transform them, Ānanda.
For the sake of even a single sentient being, the Tathāgata [acts]."
He shall remain for ninety-nine koṭis of hundreds of thousands of years.
Why is this? Ānanda, [it is because...]
"This is the domain of all Buddhas.
Ānanda, whatever task the Tathāgata ought to perform, he must certainly do it and never abandon it."
The Tathāgata remains for the duration of a kalpa,
or slightly less than a kalpa,
because he must deliver sentient beings by means of his buddha-body.
Or even more than that,
Ānanda; for this reason.
The Tathāgata converted that single sentient being through forty methods of instruction;
during the first watch of the day, he abided in the noble Dharma and attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin.
Furthermore, Ānanda,
at that time those beings spoke these verses:
"Because they do not know the past limit, the future limit, or the present,"
One who commits evil karma does not know the prior limit or the subsequent limit of phenomena;
even in the present there is nothing at all,
for the three times are equal, and therein nothing can be apprehended.
Through conceptualization there is attainment; if one is free from it, there is no attainment.
All phenomena are non-existent; thus, according to the teaching of suchness, one should abandon the perception of desire, and the perception of emptiness is likewise so.
When perception is severed, there is no conceptual differentiation;
this is called "non-existence," yet it is said that the body possesses existence.
Because of grasping, all phenomena are manifested as unattainable; therein, nothing is extinguished.
If one grasps at nirvāṇa, that very thought is a perverted grasping;
therefore, it is said that there is a thing. To speak of perception where there is none is a perversion;
to speak of non-perception where there is perception is likewise so.
Because he is free from all conceptualizations, the bhikṣu has realized non-existence;
having understood that desire, hatred, and delusion likewise exist as this non-existence,
he is called one who possesses the Dharma-eye.
I have already understood their desire; thus, in reality, there is no thing that is neither born nor extinguished.
This is well-spoken by the Great Wise One as his own conception: that all phenomena are devoid of conceptualization.
Conventionally, there is speech; therein, nothing can be apprehended.
Having spoken of emptiness as empty, that which is attained is the non-arising of name-and-form;
its intrinsic nature is the emptiness of phenomena.
Regarding the power [attained] in nirvāṇa, there are further sentient beings who attain the nirvāṇa with perception;
they perceive that all perceptions have been extinguished,
and even the perception of phenomena is likewise so.
"Neither grasping nor abandoning— this is what the Supreme Man has taught, Ānanda.
These sixty beings who dwell in Śrāvastī," so it was said.
In the past, at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
after these śrāvakas had made offerings to the Buddha,
they subsequently engaged in unrighteous activities.
They are not arhats. Frequently,
for the sake of gain and offerings, they praise themselves and exalt themselves,
yet they do not realize that they have not attained the flavor of the Dharma.
Having committed evil karma, one's faculties become impaired and diminished.
Furthermore, Ānanda,
there are five kinds of unwholesome faculties due to their inequality.
It is not that a non-friend performs the conduct of a friend. Ānanda,
there are sentient beings who are fully endowed with the five faculties.
They are unable to practice any form of service,
even deceiving their own mothers,
let alone other sentient beings.
In this Vinaya, one who possesses five types of physical characteristics and has fearful eyes may not go forth into homelessness.
Among these five types of physical characteristics, one with fearful eyes may not go forth into homelessness.
Within this Dharma and Vinaya,
one who possesses the five types of physical marks and has red eyes may not go forth.
Within this Dharma and Vinaya...
In this Vinaya, one who possesses five types of physical characteristics, such as having large red eyes,
may not go forth. In this Vinaya,
a person with five types of physical characteristics, such as being lame, may not go forth.
In this Dharma and Vinaya,
one who possesses five types of physical characteristics— such as having crooked calves— is not permitted to go forth.
In this Dharma and Vinaya...
In this Vinaya and Dharma, five types of people who are deaf may not go forth into homelessness; likewise,
five types of people with hunched backs may not go forth into homelessness.
Within this Dharma and Vinaya,
those with five types of eye defects are not permitted to go forth.
Within this Dharma and Vinaya...
One who possesses five [defects], nine fingers, or eleven fingers may not go forth.
Within this Vinaya,

Atāpā, natāpā, saniṣā, sanaṃsā— these are the four noble truths.
When the Tathāgata taught these noble truths to the sentient beings of that city, [they attained realization].
Seventy thousand beings,
far removed from dust and free from defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye. Ānanda!
Furthermore, Ānanda, there is a border village in the north;
there is a city named Niyagamaṇḍu.
Ānanda, [there...]
Ānanda, that city is half a yojana in length.
Twenty hundred thousand koṭis of people dwell in that city.
When the Tathāgata had arrived at that place,
he taught the Four Noble Truths:
namely, suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
However, regarding that city, it is said:
"Phala, Vīraka, Anuma, and Vibhūka—these are the Four Noble Truths.
The Tathāgata [taught them] for the sake of the sentient beings of that city."
When the Noble Truths were taught,
thirty thousand beings there attained the pure Dharma-eye,
free from dust and removed from defilement.
Ānanda, to the north there is another city named Cīrṇā. Ānanda.
That city was twenty yojanas in length and breadth.
The Tathāgata went to that city and preached the Four Noble Truths:
namely, suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
However, it is stated in that place:
"Vibhūta, Anama, Taga, and Tālaka— at that time,
twenty thousand beings became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye."
Ānanda, in future ages after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
these Four Noble Truths spoken here in this Middle Kingdom [shall endure].
However, at that time and place, there shall be the name of the Tathāgata’s Noble Truths. Ānanda,
in the eastern direction there is a city named Bahuputra.
It was one yojana in length and breadth.
Fourteen koṭis of sentient beings resided in that city.
The Tathāgata arrived at that city.
For the sake of those sentient beings,
he taught the Four Noble Truths— namely, suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering—
and yet, at that place, it was said:

*Pāṭimodara*, *Vimati-ccheda*, *Śani-garīśa-vigariśa*. At that time, thirty thousand sentient beings, having distanced themselves from dust and removed defilement, attained the arising of the Dharma-eye.
Ānanda, there are various nāgas and nāga kings,
namely, the Nāga King Anavatapta.

The Tathāgata went to that place for the sake of the dragon king and taught the Four Noble Truths: suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
It was at that very spot that he spoke these words.
"Aśāhu, Viśākulu, Dhanuṣya, and Saphalānan. While he was preaching the Dharma for them, that dragon king,
together with sixty-eight thousand dragons, received and upheld the five precepts.
Furthermore, by means of these Four Noble Truths,
the Tathāgata caused five thousand nāgas there,
including the Nāga King Prabhāsa, to receive and uphold the five precepts.
Furthermore, it was by means of these Four Noble Truths that the Tathāgata taught for the sake of subduing the Dragon King;
it was right there at that place.
There were twelve hundred thousand nāgas who had received and upheld the five precepts;
for them, the Tathāgata preached these Four Noble Truths to the nāga king Saṇḍaka.
There, four million nāgas observed the five precepts;
for their sake, the Tathāgata taught these Four Noble Truths to the future nāga kings.
In that place,
four million nāga kings received and upheld the five precepts,
and [taught] by means of the Four Noble Truths.
The Tathāgata spoke thus for the nāga king Śāśvata-ṛddhi; right there,
fifty-two hundred thousand nāga kings received and upheld the five precepts.
Furthermore, Ānanda, it was by means of these Four Noble Truths that the Tathāgata proclaimed and revealed them to the Naga King Viśvavarṇa.
Ānanda, that Nāga King Viśvarūpa was handsome,
pleasing, and a sight beloved by all people.
The palace of that Naga King Viśvavarṇa is seventy-two yojanas in length and breadth;
it is exquisitely adorned and a sight that delights all who behold it.
It is composed of the seven treasures,
namely gold, silver, and so forth, up to musaragalva;
the seventh is stated in brief.
For what reason is he named the Nāga King Viśvavarṇa? Ānanda,
within the precincts of that Nāga King Viśvavarṇa’s palace, there is a high terrace.
It was forty yojanas in length and breadth,
composed of blue lapis lazuli,
majestic and radiant, endowed with a magnificent appearance.
Ānanda, within that high terrace there were eight thousand seats,
composed of the seven precious substances and interspersed with golden threads.
A pure cloth covers the cushion upon his seat;
it is half a yojana in width, Ānanda.
At that time, on every part of that seat,
there sat various nāga maidens,
who were upright, beautiful, and pleasing for all to behold.
Within that terrace appeared the Nāga King Anavatapta;
all the karmic fruits and rewards experienced by the Nāga King Anavatapta were fully manifested within that terrace.
Ānanda, the Nāga King Anavatapta fully knows all the karmic fruits experienced by that Nāga King Viśvarūpa.
Those two dragon kings saw one another,
each played together,
and each experienced their respective karmic retributions.
Ānanda, that Dragon King Universal Color is also named Hard to Subdue.
Ānanda, that dragon king was also the eldest son of the Dragon King Anavatapta.
When the Tathāgata arrived there, he again preached these Four Noble Truths for him.
In that place, forty hundred thousand nāga kings observe the five precepts.
Ānanda, if the Tathāgata had not subdued those nāga kings, [this would not have been possible].
While ordinary people do not provide food and drink as alms even to the śrāvakas,
the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One,
does so for the sake of the great benefit of the multitude.
"For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to many people,
I have tamed that nāga king and caused him to receive the five precepts, Ānanda."
The Naga King Anavatapta has ten thousand sons.
Among them all is a palace where the Naga King Anupamadatta resides.
The Tathāgata caused all those nāgas to receive and uphold the five precepts.
Ānanda, there is a nāga king named Talaśu.
The Tathāgata then taught those four noble truths to them.
There, sixty thousand nāga kings received and upheld the five precepts, Ānanda.
There was a nāga king named Vipaśyin.
The Tathāgata again preached these Four Noble Truths for him;
there, sixty-four thousand nāgas received the five precepts.
Ānanda, there is a nāga king named Tālapuṭa; for his sake,
the Tathāgata has again preached these Four Noble Truths.
There, thirty thousand nāgas received the five precepts once again. Ānanda,
the Nāga King Tālapuṭa possesses a great palace.
It is twenty-four yojanas in length and breadth;
it is filled with a pool of water twenty-four yojanas deep,
possessing a beautiful color and exquisite form, which people delight in beholding.
That pond is cool, refreshing, pure, and unturbid, being exceedingly sweet. Ānanda,
at the four sides of that pond, four terraces have arisen.
Made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, it stands seven yojanas high;
suspended above that, it rests as a single pavilion,
like a multi-storied mansion.
The Tathāgata Suvikrāntaśīla also taught these Four Noble Truths to them;
at that place, ninety hundred thousand nāga kings also received the five precepts.
Ānanda, within the realm of King Gandhāra,
there is a nāga king named Elāpattra.
The Tathāgata preached these Four Noble Truths for them.
There, thirty hundred thousand nāga kings received and upheld the five precepts.
Ānanda, for the sake of Upānanda,
the Tathāgata taught these Four Noble Truths;
there, two million koṭis of nāga kings received and upheld the five precepts.
Ānanda, the Tathāgata has likewise taught these four noble truths to the Naga King Sāgara.
In that place, sixty-eight koṭis of nāgas observed the five precepts.
At that dwelling,
the Tathāgata fulfilled the observance of the precepts for all those hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nāga kings who reside in Jambudvīpa and serve as its leaders.
He likewise taught this Dharma of the Noble Truths.
However, the Tathāgata, knowing the speech, the terminology, and the expressions of the nāga kings,
likewise used those very terms to teach the Four Noble Truths.
Ānanda, therein,
for the sake of the yakṣas such as Upāriṣṭa and others,
he taught the Four Noble Truths.

Just as it is said here regarding suffering (duḥkha), the origin of suffering (samudaya), the cessation of suffering (nirodha), and the path leading to the cessation of suffering (mārga), so too it is said there:

*akhasati-ka* (Sui: "suffering"), *khavasa-ka* (Sui: "origin of suffering"), *anapana* (Sui: "cessation of suffering"), and *satapana* (Sui: "path leading to the cessation of suffering")—these were used to cover the feet of the yakṣas and others with bowls.
He taught these Four Noble Truths; therein,
for the sake of the yakṣas who were perpetually intoxicated and so forth,
he taught the Four Noble Truths.
Just as it is said here regarding suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering, so too is it said there:
*āyuṣmat*, *tāruka*, *vighna*, and *parāvasu*; furthermore, these are for the sake of the long-tongued yakṣas and others.
"I have taught these Four Noble Truths,
Ānanda, for the sake of those such as the Mālādhāra yakṣas."
The Four Noble Truths are taught;
as it is said here in this world, "Suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering,
and the path leading to the cessation of suffering," so it is expressed in that place.
Śrāṇavāsa, vāsaka, āhu, atiriviti— to the yakṣas who hold garlands and others,
he preached these Four Noble Truths. Ānanda.
Therein, for those Four Great Kings,
he taught the Four Noble Truths:
namely, suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Then, at that very place, he spoke:
"Iṇi, Miṇi, Dappa, Tāḍappa. For those Four Great Kings and others, he thus preached these Four Noble Truths.
Ānanda, when these Noble Truths were being taught,
the Four Great Kings and seven thousand devaputras [attained realization].
Distant from dust and free from defilement, they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Ānanda,
the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens spoke of the Noble Truths in this way, saying:
Up to the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
In that place it is said:
"Ānāpānasmṛti (mindfulness of breathing), ānāpānasmṛti; samudaya (origination), samudaya; nirodha (cessation), nirodha; mārga (the path), mārga, Ānanda."
When the Tathāgata taught this Noble Truth,
fifty-seven thousand devas were freed from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Ānanda, for those in the Tuṣita heaven, one should teach the Noble Truths, just as they are spoken of here,
up to the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
Then, at that place, he spoke:
"Bhīmasa, Anāgama, Tattvarava, Nyichapobumi, Ānan.
When these Noble Truths were thus proclaimed, [the earth shook].
Ānanda, among the gods of Tuṣita, six million seven hundred thousand gods attained the Dharma-eye regarding phenomena that are free from dust and defilement.
The Tathāgatas teach the Dharma through supernatural powers.
By means of this Dharma instruction, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
[teach] for the sake of the higher devas, such as the Tuṣita devas and others.
"Ānanda, when these Noble Truths were taught,
the sons of the gods and the lords of the gods [were filled with joy]."
The Tathāgata knows all the speech and all the verbal karma of the yakṣas and yakṣa kings, as well as the nāgas and nāga kings.
All those Tathāgatas know them well. Ānanda,
the Tathāgata fully knows the noble truths spoken by the asuras.
Just as it is here spoken of as the noble truths of suffering up to the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, so there it is spoken of as the noble truths, saying:
"Three anudānas, viparīyogas, asallu, and vinibaddhus. Thus he spoke of the noble truths.
The Tathāgata has taught these noble truths for the sake of the asuras;
they should be understood and known, Ānanda.
At that time, there was a city named Pratiṣṭhāna.
In that city, the Tathāgata taught the Four Noble Truths, just as they are spoken of here,
up to the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
Therein it is said:
"Bhīmadāsthanu, Anayāsticidu, Sarācūsamacāri—these are the Four Noble Truths."
When the Tathāgata preached these Noble Truths for the sake of all the sentient beings within that city,
seven thousand beings became free from dust and removed from defilement.
Within all phenomena, he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Ānanda,
this Jambudvīpa is surrounded by five hundred sub-continents as its retinue.
Each is one hundred yojanas [in extent].
Aparagoyānī also has five hundred sub-islands as its retinue,
each likewise being one hundred yojanas [in extent].
Pūrvavideha has five hundred sub-islands as its retinue,
each one hundred yojanas in extent;
Uttarakuru likewise has five hundred sub-islands as its retinue.
Each is one hundred yojanas [in extent], Ānanda.
These five hundred islands and sandbanks belonging to this Jambudvīpa are its retinue.
That is a dwelling place of non-humans,
where there are many nāgas, yakṣas, pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, and elephants,
all surrounded by their retinues and constantly engaged in mutual strife.
Yet those various beasts play with one another;
to these five classes,
the Tathāgata does not preach the Noble Truths.
Why is this? Because those sentient beings have fallen into an unfavorable state;
nevertheless, they still possess voices and breath with which they call out to one another.
The Tathāgata knows them all:
what is called "father and mother" here is called "alukapavilikāliśa" there.
What is here called "food and drink" is there called *satthānamidulū*;
what is here called "the court and friends" is there called [so-and-so].
What is called *mimdrā-tuliyā* there is called *prajñapti* here;
what is called *pāṭakā-mukhana-khi* there is [called something else] here.
In that place, there is no sound of the Buddha, no sound of the Dharma, and no sound of the Saṅgha.
Why is this? Because they have reached a state of non-familiarity with those sounds.
In this manner, the retinues of the four continents are like those of Jambudvīpa;
it should be explained in detail in this way,
up until they are unskilled in those matters.
In this sequential manner,
the Tathāgata fully knows the various modes of speech used by the people of Jambudvīpa.
Ānanda, in this Jambudvīpa,
in the north, there is a place named Sū and named Taila.
"Honey" is a name for salt;
"sugar" is a name for a woman;
"clothing" is a name for a country.
These are names of locations;
such as these, they are spoken of as being in this place.

The Tathāgata knows Sabisu in the north, as well as Parasunu, Aharīyu, Sanudeli, Gaśajalu, Gavīathu, Danabidatisṭha, Gurukhu, Nīradara, Bihiduga, Tudhara-ba, Dikhinu, Jaṭalu, Vibhasa, Parayuki, and Vihinu. The Tathāgata knows these and others as the names of the *sū* (regions) in the north. Thus the names of the northern *sū* have been completed.
Having understood various names and,
having understood their respective expressions,
[he understands] furthermore the names for oil in the north.

Mala-bhau, kuśu-ti-u, kṣimi-du-lu, viśva-du, vidha-pa-du, dhi-śa-nu, rudha-ju-śan-ni-śa-nu, kī-śa-ri, vī-ta-du-u-bi-phā-lu-kṣi-hu-tu, sattha-nu-gu, bi-śa-ku-lu, sam-ma-du-ra. These are the names of oils, such as those from the north and other directions.
The Tathāgata fully knows all various names and various expressions.
In that region, the names for honey are:

*mākṣika*, *madhu*, *sāra-kṣa*, *dīrghasittha*, *arphusamada*, *vela*, *pilita*, *pasada*, *piṅgavati*, *nāgamani*, *vimati*, *niśanudagārapa*. Such are the names for honey in the north and other directions.
The Tathāgata fully knows the names for milk in those regions:
*nisattarāṇiśce*, *nilośite*, *ditanathe*, *pilikā*, *raśanapilikā*, *himanī*, *sāuśara*, *abiraka*, *tenuvahu*, *cicahana*, *lomodua*, *himidara*, *aśaga*, *bidumanān*.
The Tathāgata fully knows such names for milk as these in the north.
Ānanda, in that place, the name for granulated sugar is [as follows].
Nidhumi khyaman kadara chiyi bha jaman dao shou da pi shaja ba ti sa t’a shou da tie shaja ba da a sa che su ka lo ka lo po ku da a nan.
The Tathāgata fully knows such names for sugar as these, and many names for honey.
Furthermore, Ānanda, among them there is a multitude;
the Tathāgata fully knows the name of salt in that place.
Vijaya | Śaṅkha-ṣaṭa | Bhavatha | Citra-miḍana-ta-ṣaha-sa | Ku-ṣaṭa-buddhara | Upaśara-saṇaka | Cili-kiri | Meru-pa-gu | Śava-sagata-sajñika | Lu-nā-ananda.
The people of the northern regions refer to salt by such names;
the Tathāgata knows that there are even more numerous [names] than these, Ānanda.
The people there have such names for curd as these,
which the Tathāgata knows them all:
Kharabi, Dudadi, Sukiki, Sukise, Dangnati, Saghati, Bibhuti, Anihi, Gabada, Rabapu, Pasaphali, Sadase, Dadiana.
The Tathāgata fully knows such languages of the people in those regions,
as well as many other words and expressions.
All languages, all names,
and all bases of realization.
In this place and that place,
the Tathāgata speaks the Dharma with such words and phrases, Ānanda.
There is a name of such a form:

Balenabadevavāhasatsadamantrorecayaṃtudamudadhanugadubibhagmūatāmrapuñjaridulūupayakṣitihetu-kātuparodipavadaliśaru-aśiñjanayu-paṭiṣṭha-paṭihāmūla-bipusṭaku-u-rākujetata-tiśa-tiśaci-niśanu-satijavadaliśi-nimidu-kiñcanu-lupāvānanda.
Such are the names for places, forms,
and so forth; the sounds produced by those people,
their various utterances, and their various names.
Among all those who have attained realization and among all people,
in every such place and within the speech and terminology of all people throughout every land.
The Tathāgata fully knows all these things:
the worldly speech and the worldly names of the world,
which increase even further beyond this.
Ānanda, this aggregate of the five skandhas serves as darkness for all sentient beings who lack the eye.
Because faith increases, it is said that the Tathāgata knows and sees that form as it truly is.
How does the Tathāgata know form as it truly is?
To say that the formless is form—
this is called the Tathāgata’s knowing form as it truly is and seeing form as it truly is.
It is so, it is so. Because ordinary beings lack the eye of wisdom,
they are unable to know or see the true nature of form.
What is called the true mark of form?
It is that all forms are without permanence;
this is because they possess the nature of impermanence.
To say that all forms are impermanent is to speak of form;
the Tathāgata does not describe this as "arising.
It is, for example, like a person whose body is afflicted with a malignant ulcer.
Just as one prepares various medicines to treat those sores,
even so it is with ordinary worldlings.
Ānanda, form arises through the increase of improper mindfulness,
because it is shrouded by karma, afflictions, and ignorance.
There are ten names for sleep:
*pimati*, *sittiṇamitu*, *savida*, *arasa*, *macibhajatu*, *asiri*, *anapali*, *sa-u*, *paluyudano*, and *hani-anan*.
Ānanda, having known these ten names for sleep,
the Tathāgata further increased [the categories] therein.
If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas,
or upāsikās who know such places and know such matters.
One should know that such a person, possessing such a body of names and such a body of phrases,
will not fall into a state of confusion and will be fully accomplished in pure verbal karma.
Ānanda, based on this foundation, the Tathāgata,
the World-Honored One, possesses four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
The Tathāgata fully knows and fully awakens to all various languages and various modes of expression;
regarding these matters, he is thus.
Having trained in names, phrases,
and syllables, one shall attain manifold wisdom and boundless wisdom.
One attains right mindfulness,
attains right mental intention,
and attains right orientation.
One attains right contentment.
One attains unsurpassed erudition that is not learned from others,
which is like the great ocean, inexhaustible.
For what reason?
Ānanda, I recall that in the past, at this very seat, within the realm of empty space.
Sixty-eight hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-Bhagavāns have spoken this sūtra;
those Tathāgatas—
Ānanda, for those śrāvakas who are worthy recipients of the Dharma,
the Tathāgata has expounded this sutra for their sake.
If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas,
or upāsikās who receive and uphold this dhāraṇī chapter,
and who cultivate it with great excellence, reciting and chanting it until they have mastered it.
He was then able to receive four thousand verses;
having heard them, he could retain them,
and having retained them, he did not forget them.
Ānanda, if one is able to receive and uphold these words and phrases,
yet does not contemplate them for a hundred years.
Later, as he desired, his eloquence was restored.
After the Buddha had spoken these words,
the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!
Having realized such a Dharma as this,
the Tathāgata acts for the sake of all sentient beings."
"It increases knowledge, increases mindfulness, increases wisdom, increases eloquence, and increases progress, Blessed One.
If there is anyone who can receive this Dharma-text..."
“Having received and upheld it, how much merit will they obtain?
After he had spoken these words, Ānanda—
The Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Do not conceive limited conceptions regarding the Tathāgata or within the Tathāgata’s teaching.
If, within this teaching of the Tathāgata..."
Whether as a householder or one who has gone forth,
they receive, maintain, read, and recite even a four-line verse spoken by the Buddhas.
For the sake of self-discipline,
and for the sake of illuminating for oneself the principle of true nature,
the Tathāgata does not set a limit upon that mass of merit.
How much more so for one who fully receives and upholds this dharma-text of the dhāraṇī,
and explains it to others without deficiency in either its words or its meaning;
the mass of merit of such a person is immeasurable.
Why is this? Ānanda,
after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, this Dharma-fundamental will [endure] for a hundred years.
At that time, Jambudvīpa was most excellently manifested.
Śakra, King of the Devas, constantly came to this Jambudvīpa;
yet, there were places where this Dharma-fundamental Sūtra had been destroyed, lost, or corrupted.
At that time, Ānanda, because Śakra, King of Devas, assists them,
they are able to receive and practice [the teachings] without letting them be lost or destroyed.
Now, because of the influence of Māra, once this root of the Dharma has been transcribed,
it shall sink into the earth during the four hundred years [following].
Ānanda, five hundred years after that time,
there will be many sentient beings who, having performed various meritorious deeds, will be born into this world.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Candra.
He possessed great majesty and great power.
That bhikṣu Candra—
Within my birthplace, the great city of Kapilavastu,
this sūtra shall emerge from that location and be widely circulated and manifested for the sake of sentient beings.
And when that later dharma is extinguished,
having appeared and shone forth, it quickly vanishes again, Ānanda.
Ānanda, it is like an oil lamp whose oil is exhausted while the wick remains burning at both ends;
having manifested its light, it shall soon be extinguished. Ānanda.
It is so, it is so. The teaching of the Tathāgata shall appear in the world during the final five hundred years.
Having manifested this illumination, it shall soon be extinguished again. Ānanda,
at that time there will be many hundreds of unrighteous and evil dharmas.
Appearing in the world, at that time,
whether as householders or as those who have gone forth from the home life.
All men and women whose minds are entangled and disturbed by Māra Pāpīyān—
those sentient beings, regarding the perfectly complete awakening of a Buddha...
One gives rise to the perception of unreality;
one gives rise to the perception of wrong view;
and within the perception of wrong view, one gives rise to the perception of right view.
Ānanda, observe even those who are not virtuous persons,
whether they be monastics or householders.
There will be great loss and diminution,
Ānanda. It is as if,
for example, there were a person who desired his own benefit, desired his own happiness, and desired to be free from fear.
He took an iron staff and struck his own head with it.
Ānanda, what do you think?
"Does that person bring benefit or lack benefit?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One..."
What benefit could there be for that person?
That foolish man,
having struck his own head with that iron club, immediately met his end.
"There is such a possibility.
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda:
"So it is, so it is."
At that time, whether one is a layperson or a monastic,
those who wish to cultivate meritorious deeds should recite the words of the Buddha.
Desiring to increase their knowledge,
they instead abandon bodhicitta,
studying the scriptures of non-Buddhist traditions and clinging to their recollections thereof.
Because they recite and study the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths,
they slander the words of the Buddha;
after casting off this body, they shall fall into hell.
Those who are foolish and devoid of wisdom fall into the Great Avīci Hell;
having entered that place of no respite,

and because they will revile the Tathāgata’s teaching, thinking, "I shall become a Buddha."

mixed with the speech of non-Buddhists and worshipped the sun.

This third karma leads toward hell.
What is the fourth type of sensual conduct that leads to falling into hell?
It is the absence of roots of goodness.
What is it that constitutes the absence of roots of goodness?
It is when sentient beings delight in practicing various sensual desires and matters of lust.
One is covered and overwhelmed by desire;
desire is a dense thicket,
a place of rivers and ponds.
The place of the brothel;
the place of evil adornment;
the place of slaughter.

it is like a man who has two sons,

nor will they observe the precepts.

What is that power of extensive learning?

Furthermore, what is this so-called "agent of naming"?
An agent cannot be apprehended,
because that which is produced by an agent cannot be apprehended.
Even therein, it cannot be found.
It is impossible for there to be a name [for that which does not exist].

whatever notion of non-renunciation arises therein is born of desire.
He desires to emerge from it because of many thoughts of desire;
because of these many thoughts of desire, he is bound by desire.
Overwhelmed by desire,
they associate with the impure, take pleasure in the impure,
and delight in false speech.
Like a dog gnawing at a dry bone,
dwelling constantly amidst desire in an impure place— this is called the perception of not having gone forth.
When such a person, remaining a householder, indulges in various sensual pleasures, [it is as described above].
Because of the conditions of desire and due to excessive greed for desires, for the sake of those very desires,
one performs various kinds of evil karma; when the body perishes and life ends, one is reborn in the woeful states or in the hells.
Therein they undergo extreme suffering and affliction;
because they experience such suffering and affliction, they are neither joyful nor happy;
and because they lack joy and happiness, they are entirely without pleasure or delight.
This is the fourth thought of not going forth and the state of lack of joy.
Among these, any thought of false views arising from conceptual discrimination is a great evil; it is not that it is not evil.
If it were not non-evil, it would be the most extreme evil.
If it were the most extreme evil, one would grasp at extreme views;
if one grasps at extreme views, that is itself an extreme view.
If one holds extreme views, they are thereby breaking the precepts;
if they break the precepts, they destroy their roots of goodness and remain dormant within the roots of unwholesomeness.
If one conforms to latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), that itself becomes grasping (*upādāna*);
if there is grasping, that itself constitutes the act of grasping;
if there is the act of grasping, that itself is terror (*bhaya*).
If one is terrified, they will fall into hell;
having fallen into hell, they will undergo extreme suffering and affliction.
Having undergone such extreme suffering, they will find neither joy nor pleasure.
Because there is no joy or bliss, one becomes attached to false views;
this constitutes arising through conceptual discrimination.
The perception of false views constitutes the five perceptions of non-joy.
Among these various perceptions, there is only one perception that can give rise to a lack of joy.
Which single perception is it that can give rise to it?
That is to say, they do not give rise to reverence toward all phenomena.
Because they lack reverence, they do not engage in cultivation and study.
Because they do not study, their wisdom does not increase within the Prajñāpāramitā.
Having thus lacked wisdom, he will become a deluded worldling.
This is what constitutes a worldling:
namely, the five kinds of unpleasant perceptions.
These five perceptions and practices are called "non-delight.
Ānanda, you should know that at that time,
during the five hundred years when the True Dharma is perishing.
There are some bhikṣus who have no reverence for the True Dharma;

Because there is no growth within Prajñā,
one shall thereby attain such a dharma as this:
namely, the absence of cognition.
Because of a lack of wisdom, one does not understand the causes within such phenomena,

If one becomes estranged from such true dharmas as these, [the consequences will follow].
They do not uphold the true Dharma of the Buddhas;

Ānanda, for this reason I tell you, I declare to you:

Ānanda, it is as if in this trichiliocosm, atop the kalpavṛkṣa trees, there were all manner of garments fully provided;

In order to take the garment, he went to where the garment from the beginning of the kalpa was located.
At that moment, seeing the garment from the beginning of the kalpa, he touched it with his hand;
having touched it, he was struck with terror and immediately fell into remorse.
Having become terrified, he spoke these false and deceptive words: "What is this?
How subtle it is! How delicate it is!"
Then, out of fear, he fled with great speed.
Another person saw him fleeing and said to him, "O man!"
"Why are you fleeing in such terror?
He replied, "O Noble Sir," and so on.
If you wish to know for what purpose I am thus rushing about,

yet you will neither be able to discern it nor see it.
That person spoke to him again, saying:

"For what purpose are you running about like this?
He replied, "I cannot remain still;

"But now, while I am running,
you shall follow behind me and accompany my path; then,

Then that man, employing skillful means,
ran after him in accordance with his speed;
as that man was thus running, [the other] pursued him.
Without ceasing or resting, he spoke these words:

you are hanging there upon that tree in such various colors, suspended from it."
I reached out my hand, wishing to take that garment;

"You do not know that this is the garment from the beginning of the eon;

"You should come;

It is so, it is so. In future ages, there will be bhikṣus who hear the name of such a sūtra as this.

Thus it was, thus it was.

Among these, what are the five sufferings?
These are called the five types of suffering: bodily suffering, mental suffering, the suffering of karmic maturation, worldly volitional suffering, and the suffering of conceptualization.
Among these, what is bodily suffering?
If one forms the notion of a body,
then having such a body, one is deluded;
lacking discernment, one possesses no knowledge.
If one does not grasp at the pain of the body as real within the very nature of the body,
this is the ultimate pain.
Among these, what is it?
This is mental pain.
Because the mind is the leader of all actions, there is mental pain;
furthermore, there is also physical pain.
If one contemplates all phenomena with the mind,

What is the fundamental, vast, and stabilizing stone?
That which is called the fundamental, vast,
and stabilizing stone is precisely craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Ānanda, regarding the name "love for possessions" as it occurs among various countries and villages,

He has such names as these:

These are the names for craving;
because of these, there shall be heartache,

Due to conceptualization and discrimination,
whatever karma and sensation exist therein constitute this outflowing karma.
Among these, what are the outflows?
They are bodily action, verbal action, and mental action. Why is this so?
Because the mind is predominant and because the mind is primary,
there subsequently arise speech, words, and names.
Regarding all wholesome bodily, verbal, and mental actions therein,
even the Tathāgata describes those mental actions as being with outflows (sāsrava). Why is this?
That itself is karma.
If there were such karma that did not receive its retribution and yet exhausted the afflictions,
the Tathāgata would say that karma is exhausted and the afflictions are exhausted.
Among these, when all the ripened fruits have been exhausted,
one should experience those that are either black or white;
whatever is experienced therein is precisely suffering.
If that which is suffering is itself painful feeling,
then because of that painful feeling, there exists a locus of pain that abides based upon its foundation.
Furthermore, in brief, there are five kinds of painful feeling.
As the Tathāgata has taught:

They are within the afflictions of the cyclic flow of birth and death.
Hell-beings, animals, the world of Yama, humans, and devas—

Within this, what are the five kinds of severance of pain? They are: the severance of pain through seeing the Buddha; the severance of pain through hearing the Dharma; [the severance of pain through attending upon the Saṃgha; the severance of pain through practicing giving; and the severance of pain through cultivating morality].
Seeing the cessation of suffering through the Sangha;
the cessation of suffering through practicing in accordance with the Dharma;
and the cessation of suffering through the quiescence of all phenomena.
These are the five cessations of suffering.
Furthermore, there are another five cessations of all sufferings.
What are these five?
A virtuous friend cuts off all pains.
One who does not give rise to afflictions cuts off all pains.
One who is exhorted to uphold the prohibitive precepts cuts off all pains.
Not committing the deeds of immediate retribution cuts off all suffering;
extinguishing all modes of existence cuts off all suffering.
These are the five ways of cutting off all suffering.
Furthermore, there are another five kinds of abandoning all pains.
What are these five?
They are the merchant’s skillful means for successfully accomplishing the abandonment of all pains.
Dwelling at will within the kingdom, one cuts off all suffering.
Filially supporting one's parents, one cuts off all suffering.
Leaving home and renouncing the world for the sake of awakening, one cuts off all suffering.
Abandoning all desires and severing all pains—
these are the five ways of severing all pains.
Among these, what are the five darknesses?
The five deeds of immediate retribution constitute darkness. What are these five?
Killing one’s mother.
Patricide, killing an arhat,
and causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
To draw blood from a Tathāgata with an evil mind—these constitute the five kinds of darkness.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of darkness regarding rebirth destinies (*gati*). What are these five?
The darkness of hell;
the darkness of the animal realm;
the darkness of the world of Yama.
Being born in a remote place is darkness; being deceived by others is darkness.
These are the five kinds of darkness.
Among them, which are the five blind spots of darkness?
Grasping at a self is a state of blinding darkness.
To give rise to extreme craving and attachment toward sensual desires is blinding darkness.
Sloth and indolence are blinding darkness.
Excessive sleep is a state of blinding darkness;
not reaching one's destination is a state of blinding darkness.
These constitute the five states of blinding darkness. Among them, what are the five rapid waves?
Ill-will is a swift wave;
one who has attained the fourth dhyāna may form the thought,
"I am an arhat."
Arrogance and self-exaltation are rapid waves.
Clinging to one's low birth because of what has already been attained—which was previously unattained—is a rapid wave.
To maintain precepts and give rise to pride on account of those precepts is a rapid wave.
Because one does not extinguish the afflictions, one grasps at the rapid waves within conditioned existence;
these constitute the five rapid waves.
Among them, what are the five rākṣasa abysses?
Ignorance is a deep abyss;
sloth and torpor are a deep abyss;
the cyclic flow of birth and death is a deep abyss.
The abyss of ignorance and the abyss of craving—
among these, the latter is the foremost abyss.
Regarding those who wander within the three realms,
among these five abysses, which are the five kinds of rākṣasīs?
They are the rākṣasī of evil associates.
The rākṣasī born in uninhabited places;
the rākṣasī who attends upon women; the rākṣasī of unwholesome thoughts;
and the rākṣasī of the notion of self.
These are the five rākṣasa abysses.
Within those five rākṣasa abysses,
"karma" refers to serving women.
Among these, what are the five waves of conduct that are difficult to cross?
They are the waves of conduct of the desire realm that are difficult to cross,
and the waves of conduct of the form realm that are difficult to cross.
The formless realm is a difficult-to-cross wave-like course.
If one does not observe these three realms and lacks right mindfulness, it is a difficult-to-cross wave-like course.
When those beings with improper mindfulness seek after pleasure, they cannot know their destination.
These are the five difficult-to-cross waves of conduct.
Why are they called the difficult-to-cross waves of conduct?
Because they are places where it is difficult for them to arise and difficult for them to abide.
Therefore, they are said to move like waves.
Among these, what are the five states of deficiency? They are:

there is a deficiency in worldly rewards;

Spiritual friends are scarce;

It gives birth to all pure and white dharmas;
it does not dwell far from the Buddhas,

He is the most closely dwelling. Who is "close"?
Such as the Elder Śāriputra was to Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

In whatever place one is born and in all locations, there is always great wisdom.

That which is called great wisdom is as follows:

He is able to establish others in that state of great learning;

Skillfully knowing the retribution of karma—

At the time of death, one should take up the mental recollection of all phenomena.
